narration: A figure comparing two deepfake-detection pipelines. The upper blue panel is the existing method; the legend marks a circled minus for the absolute difference and a circled ring for concatenation.
The first stage of the existing method starts from an input image x, the photograph being tested as real or generated.
x is pushed through a frozen diffusion model, an encoder that compresses it and a decoder that rebuilds it.
The diffusion model returns a reconstruction x prime. The first stage ends here, and its weights never change.
The second stage is trained separately. It receives only the finished pair of images, x and its reconstruction x prime.
The two are subtracted and the absolute difference is taken, giving the reconstruction error map x rec.
A classifier reads that error map alone and predicts whether the image is real or generated.
But the two stages never talk to each other. The first stage is trained without interaction with the second, so its reconstruction is not optimised for detection.
The lower yellow panel is the proposed method. Everything inside it is trained end to end, as a single network.
The same input x also passes through FMRE, a module that produces a pseudo version of the image, x pse.
Both x and x pse go through the shared diffusion model, which reconstructs them into x prime and x prime pse.
Two absolute differences are taken in parallel: x against x prime gives x rec, and x pse against x prime pse gives x pse rec.
The two error maps are concatenated and handed to the classifier, which outputs the real or generated decision.
Because gradients flow back through the whole chain, the diffusion stage is tuned for the detector, giving better alignment between reconstruction and classification.
